author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: In a future ruled by a small cabal of 'id bloc' industrial leaders who maintain power through an all-female Agency of psychic 'Immune' investigators hunting down parakinetic mutants ('P-K's) -- individuals whose delusions can warp reality around them -- industrialist John Eggerton is targeted by a random loyalty check and flees rather than submit to a mind-probe, terrified of being exposed as P-K himself.
page_summary:
In a future ruled by a small cabal of 'id bloc' industrial leaders who maintain power through an all-female Agency of psychic 'Immune' investigators hunting down parakinetic mutants ('P-K's) -- individuals whose delusions can warp reality around them -- industrialist John Eggerton is targeted by a random loyalty check and flees rather than submit to a mind-probe, terrified of being exposed as P-K himself. Denied help by his fellow bloc leaders, who consider the Agency their own necessary tool against a graver threat, Eggerton tracks down the Agency server who nearly caught him, hoping to accept her notice and throw himself on official mercy. He finds her at a party hosted by an ordinary Commerce Institute clerk, Jay Richards, who has secretly been growing living jet-transport ships from a plant in his backyard -- his own long-hidden P-K delusion, spectacularly actualized. When Richards unveils his 'creation' before the horrified party guests, Eggerton, not even a mutant himself, instantly and correctly identifies him as P-K and shoots him dead, realizing in that moment that ordinary, non-immune people can recognize a P-K's delusion for what it is simply by seeing it from the outside -- rendering the entire Agency apparatus obsolete and replacing it with mutual, universal peer surveillance.

**Why it matters.** The story's central irony is that its own protagonist may be exactly the kind of person the Agency exists to catch, and yet it is Eggerton -- fleeing his own possible diagnosis all story long -- who delivers the story's fatal, confident verdict on someone else's reality. His closing insight, that 'consensus gentium' (ordinary people comparing notes) can detect delusion better than any specialized telepathic apparatus, is framed as a triumphant discovery that will let the ruling id bloc dismantle the Agency and replace it with universal mutual surveillance -- an outcome the story presents with real ambivalence, since it amounts to converting an entire society into an informal but total policing network, achieved at the cost of one innocent, joyfully creative man's casual murder.

*Eggerton's final act -- literally flapping his arms and flying home under his own unassisted power, having apparently gained parakinetic ability himself from the same radiation or process afflicting others -- closes the story on the strong implication that the man who just diagnosed and executed a P-K is, in fact, becoming one himself.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: Eggerton's flight from the loyalty check, his failed appeal to his fellow industrial leaders, and a chance encounter that reveals a startling new method of detecting P-K's
movements: Industrialist John Eggerton evades a routine loyalty check by the all-female Agency, terrified he may himself be an undiagnosed parakinetic mutant.

Denied protection by his fellow id bloc leaders, who value the Agency as their own instrument of control, Eggerton tracks down the Agency server to formally accept his notice and submit to investigation.

At a party, Eggerton witnesses ordinary clerk Jay Richards unveil a fully-grown jet transport ship, secretly cultivated as a plant -- an obvious P-K delusion made real -- and, killing Richards on sight, realizes that any group of ordinary people, simply by comparing notes, can detect a P-K's warped reality without any Agency or telepath required.
structure.point_of_view: third person, alternating between Eggerton's mounting paranoia and Doris Sorrel's own weary professional perspective as an Agency investigator, converging at the party where both threads resolve simultaneously.
structure.central_device: A society entirely dependent on a specialized detection apparatus (a telepathic, all-female Agency) to identify a threat that turns out, in the story's final twist, to be detectable by ordinary collective human judgment all along -- a solution hiding in plain sight that costs an innocent, delusional man his life the moment it is discovered.

characters.name: John Eggerton
characters.note: His entire arc -- flight, appeal, and eventual violent epiphany -- is driven by uncertainty about his own nature rather than confirmed guilt; the story never actually confirms or denies whether Eggerton himself is P-K, leaving his climactic insight morally ambiguous rather than triumphantly vindicating.

characters.name: Doris Sorrel
characters.note: Her mundane, work-weary perspective on a job she finds tedious and unglamorous humanizes the Agency's otherwise fearsome institutional presence, and her own marriage and party-going life root the story's speculative premise in ordinary domestic texture.

characters.name: Jay Richards
characters.role: an undiagnosed parakinetic, the story's tragic figure
characters.note: His years of secret, joyful cultivation of living spacecraft -- described with genuine tenderness as his one true creative outlet against a stifling desk job -- makes his sudden, casual execution the story's most unsettling moment, since he is guilty of nothing but an unrecognized, private eccentricity finally made visible.

characters.name: Townsand
characters.note: His cold, self-interested defense of the Agency as 'our instrument,' necessary to prevent P-K's from becoming a competing majority, articulates the ruling class's actual priority: not justice, but maintained control by whatever apparatus is currently convenient.

settings.name: The Commerce Institute and id bloc hall
settings.note: Corporate and political power centers whose leaders treat the loyalty-detection apparatus as their own tool for self-preservation rather than as a genuinely impartial system of justice.

settings.name: Jay Richards's backyard
settings.note: The site of the story's central reveal -- a fully-grown, functional jet transport cultivated as a garden plant -- and of Richards's sudden death the moment his private creative world becomes visible to others.

motifs: A ruling class maintaining a specialized detection apparatus less out of principle than out of self-interested convenience, readily defended or abandoned as circumstances require
A hidden creative or delusional talent, nurtured privately and joyfully for years, destroyed instantly the moment it becomes visible to an unprepared audience
A solution to a systemic social problem (detecting P-K's) that turns out to require no special apparatus at all, only ordinary collective human observation
Violence enacted with total moral confidence by a character whose own claim to normalcy is never actually verified by the story

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No commentary by Dick on this specific story was found in this evidence pass. (A search hit under this title was actually John Brunner's 1986 introduction essay, misattributed by a heading-extraction artifact in the source corpus, and is excluded here as not genuine commentary on this story.)

open_questions: Is Eggerton ever confirmed or denied as P-K within the story? The ending's implication (he can fly) suggests yes, but this is left entirely to inference.

Is there documented commentary from Dick on the story's closing image of universal mutual surveillance replacing specialized institutional detection -- is this framed as a genuine improvement or a further, more total form of control?
Is this story ever discussed alongside Dick's other P-K/parakinetic fiction (e.g., the Eye in the Sky-adjacent material) as part of a broader treatment of delusion made literally real?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
